short: The most numerous British tank of the war, and the workhorse of Cambrai.
full:
The Mark IV kept the rhomboid hull of Mother and fixed what the Somme and Arras had exposed. Armour was thickened to defeat the German K bullet; the petrol tank was moved outside the hull at the rear, so that a hit no longer sprayed the crew compartment with fuel; and the sponsons could be swung inboard, letting a tank travel by rail without being partly dismantled first. Most carried an unditching beam, a baulk of timber chained across both tracks and dragged under the tank to give it purchase when it bogged.

Production from May 1917 reached 1,220 machines: 420 male, 595 female and 205 unarmed tank tenders. Around sixty led the attack at Messines on 7 June 1917, the mud of Third Ypres then largely defeated the type, and some 460 formed the mass of the assault at Cambrai in November. A Mark IV male fought the first tank-versus-tank action at Villers-Bretonneux in April 1918. Captured Mark IVs served the German army in greater numbers than its own A7V ever did.
